title: Festivals around the world: seven short texts
texts: Every spring, millions of people in India throw coloured powder at one another to celebrate the end of winter. Strangers, neighbours and relatives are all fair targets, and by midday the streets look like a giant painting. The festival is also a day for ending old quarrels, and people visit friends to share sweets. Music and dancing continue until late in the evening.

Each August, a quiet Scottish capital becomes the biggest arts festival in the world. Comedians perform in pubs, actors in cellars and musicians on the pavement. Anybody can take part, which means that a show may attract an audience of three or three hundred. Performers often lose money, but they return year after year for the chance of being discovered.

In Mexico, families do not avoid the subject of death. At the beginning of November they decorate graves with orange flowers and put photographs, favourite food and even toys on altars at home. The mood is cheerful rather than sad: relatives tell stories about those who have gone and believe that for one night the dead return to visit.

Although it is called Oktoberfest, this Munich event actually begins in September, when the weather is better. It started in 1810 as a wedding party for a prince, and the guests enjoyed it so much that it was repeated every year. Today about six million visitors drink beer from enormous glasses and listen to brass bands in tents that seat thousands.

The Chinese New Year celebrations end on the fifteenth day with a festival of lanterns. Thousands of paper lanterns, shaped like animals and flowers, hang along the streets, and children carry glowing ones through the crowds. People also try to solve riddles written on the lanterns, and the winners receive small prizes. The streets stay crowded until after midnight.

For four days before Lent, Rio de Janeiro dances. Samba schools spend the whole year making costumes and floats, and in the huge Sambadrome stadium they compete for the title of champion. The parades are shown on television, but the real atmosphere is on the streets, where anyone can join in free of charge. Foreign tourists often book hotels a year in advance.

In Russia, the last week before Lent is the time for pancakes. Round and golden, they stand for the sun, and people eat them with butter, jam or caviar. Other customs include sleigh rides, snowball fights and the burning of a straw figure that represents winter, while everybody enjoys the first sunny days of the year.
discuss: Which of these festivals would you most like to visit? Why?
What is the biggest festival or celebration in your town or region?
Why do people all over the world enjoy festivals?
